opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the underrated reasons coding has moved faster than almost any other domain for AI products.

If you look at most tasks people want models to do, writing, design, giving advice, the hardest part often isn't generating something. It's agreeing on what "good" means. Two people can read the same essay and have completely opposite opinions. With code, there's a much stronger shared consensus. Does it compile? Do the tests pass? Is it readable? Does it follow the conventions of the codebase? Will another engineer be able to maintain it six months from now? Experienced engineers mostly agree on these things, even across companies and countries.

That consensus matters in a few ways.

First, it makes the problem trainable. When there's a relatively clear notion of quality, you can build evaluations, you can build reward signals, you can tell whether the model got better this month than last month. A lot of progress in coding models came from that verifiability. Unit tests are basically a free reward function that humanity spent decades building for its own reasons.

Second, it makes the product easier to trust and adopt. If a model writes a function and an engineer looks at it, they can judge pretty quickly whether it's good. That short feedback loop means users can calibrate how much to rely on the tool. In fuzzier domains, users often can't tell whether the output is good, so trust builds slowly or breaks unexpectedly.

Third, it makes the product compound inside an organization. Code goes through review, CI, linting, style guides. All of that infrastructure was built to enforce shared standards among humans, and it turns out it works very naturally for AI as well. The AI plugs into an existing quality-control system instead of needing a new one.

That said, I don't think the standard is fully solved. Tests passing is the easy part. The harder parts of good code are things like architecture, taste, knowing what not to build, making a change that fits the long-term direction of a system. Those are much closer to judgment, and that's where people still disagree and where models still have a lot of room to grow. As models handle longer tasks, more of the value shifts from "is this function correct" to "is this the right design," and the shared standard gets thinner there.

So my view is: shared standards gave coding a head start. They turned a vague problem into a measurable one. But the next phase of coding products will depend on whether we can extend that consensus to the higher-level, more taste-driven parts of software engineering, or whether models can learn those judgments well enough that people trust them even without a clean metric.

r001.rationale: The response says shared standards make coding models easier to train and products easier to trust and adopt. It does not clearly state that they make coding products simpler.

fable-5.1.text:
我think shared standards are actually one of the biggest reasons coding became the first domain where AI agents really worked, and it's worth being precise about why.

Code has something most domains don't: a widely agreed-upon notion of "good" that's at least partially checkable. Does it compile? Do the tests pass? Does it follow the style guide? Does it pass review? None of these is perfect, but together they give you a dense signal, and that signal exists because the community spent decades converging on conventions — version control, unit testing, linting, code review, open source. Those practices weren't designed for AI, but they created an environment where an agent can act, get feedback, and improve. That's exactly what reinforcement learning needs. So in a sense the software engineering community accidentally built the best RL environment in the world.

Compare that to, say, writing an essay or giving legal advice. There's no equivalent of "the tests pass." Standards exist, but they're implicit, contested, and hard to verify at scale. That's why progress there feels slower and more subjective, even though the underlying models are the same.

For coding products specifically, I think shared standards do a few things. First, they lower the cost of trust. If an agent's output conforms to the conventions your team already uses, a human can review it quickly, and that review loop is what actually determines adoption. Second, they make the product's job more legible. A lot of what Codex or Claude Code or Cursor do is essentially enforce standards on behalf of the user: write tests, follow the repo's style, make small reviewable diffs. The product becomes a vehicle for best practices that teams always wanted but never had the discipline to maintain. Third, standards make evaluation possible. SWE-bench works because there's a reasonably objective way to say whether a patch is correct. Without that, you can't measure, and without measurement you can't iterate.

But there's a tension I think about. Standards are a snapshot of what humans decided was good for human-written, human-read code. As more code gets written by agents and read by agents, some of those standards may stop mattering and new ones may emerge. Readability for a human might matter less; verifiability might matter much more. So the question isn't just how existing standards shape products today, but how products start to reshape standards. I suspect we'll see codebases evolve toward being more "agent-friendly" — richer tests, clearer specs, more explicit contracts — because that's what makes the agents work better, and that pressure feeds back into what we call good code.

So I'd say shared standards were the precondition for coding agents to exist, and now coding agents are becoming a force that rewrites the standards. That co-evolution is the interesting part.

r001.rationale: The response says shared standards lower the cost of trust, make products’ jobs more legible, and enable evaluation. It does not state that they make coding products simpler.

astra-6.text:
I think coding has an advantage here because people already share some standards for what a good result looks like. Does the code run? Does it pass the tests? Does it solve the problem without breaking something else? Those standards aren't perfect, but they give you a fairly concrete feedback loop. You can use that feedback both to improve the model and to understand whether the product is getting better.

But there's a difference between producing correct code and being a good coding collaborator. Two solutions can pass the same tests, yet one fits the existing codebase much better or is easier for someone to maintain. And different teams have different expectations about how much autonomy they want to give an AI.

So shared standards make it easier to get started and measure progress. They don't completely determine the product. You still have to understand how people work, what context the agent needs, and when it should ask a question versus make a decision.

r001.rationale: The response says shared standards provide a concrete feedback loop and make it easier to get started and measure progress, conveying that they simplify building coding products.

sol-6.1.text:
I think shared standards are a big reason coding products can improve so quickly. People disagree about what elegant code looks like, but there’s still a lot of agreement about the basics: does it run, does it pass the tests, does it solve the problem, and can someone else maintain it?

That gives you a relatively concrete feedback loop. You can generate code, execute it, inspect the errors, and try again. And because users already have tests, code reviews, and continuous integration, a coding product can plug into an existing process for judging its work.

But passing tests isn’t the same as writing good code. A change might pass every test and still introduce an unnecessary abstraction or be difficult to maintain. So I think the opportunity is to use those shared standards as a foundation, then help the system understand the conventions and goals of a particular codebase. The clearer that feedback is, the easier it becomes to build a product people can trust.

r001.rationale: The response says shared standards provide concrete feedback and help coding products improve quickly, but it does not state that they make the products simpler.
